claim.primary_observation: First Chronicles 16:36 ends with the gathered people saying “Amen” and praising YHWH; its wording closely matches Psalm 106:48. The surrounding hymn also draws on material found in Psalms 105, 96, and 106.
claim.scholarly_interpretation: Longacre argues that 1 Chronicles 16:36 preserves Psalm 106:48 in its role as the doxology closing book four of the Psalter. He reads this reuse, together with other Psalm material in the hymn, as evidence that the Chronicler knew a five-book collection. He acknowledges proposals that the doxology originally belonged to Psalm 106 itself and leaves open the possibility that individual psalms entered the collection later; the exact date of Chronicles is also uncertain.

claim.primary_observation: Revelation 13:11–18 describes a second beast that exercises delegated authority, promotes worship of the first beast, makes an image, and links allegiance to buying and selling. The vision does not name a Roman office, priesthood, city, or social class.
claim.scholarly_interpretation: Friesen accepts a general relationship between the land beast and Roman imperial cults, then argues from inscriptions and the social setting of Roman Asia that the image evokes elite families operating through a network of provincial and local cult offices, municipal representatives, priesthoods, and public events. He reviews narrower proposals such as a single priesthood or provincial council but argues that the symbol is not a one-to-one cipher. The inscriptions document institutions and elite participation; they do not by themselves prove that every element of the vision maps directly to a specific historical actor or that worship was uniformly enforced across the empire.
